title: Youth perspectives on polarisation: When does difference become division?
content:
From Finland to Armenia and Palestine, young people encounter polarisation in different forms. Yet across these contexts, similar questions emerge about trust, belonging, participation and the spaces available for dialogue. These themes were at the heart of CMI’s webinar that brought together young voices to reflect on how divisions shape their societies and what role young people can play in addressing them.

The webinar, organised as part of the annual Youth Peace Week Finland’s programme, explored how polarisation affects young people in everyday life and how they navigate increasingly divided social and political environments. The discussion featured youth worker and peacebuilder Liana Vahanyan from Armenia, communications professional and researcher Atta Khaled from Palestine, and Finnish youth activist Heta Uhtio. The conversation was moderated by CMI’s Project Officer Shekeba Ahmadi and can be watched through a recording.

title: German innovation award recognises CMI’s pioneering digital approach to peacemaking
content:
The Round Table for Mediation and Conflict Management of the German Economy (RTMKM) has named CMI the winner of its 2026 Innovation Prize for Mediation and Conflict Management at an award ceremony in Frankfurt am Main on 22 September.

CMI – Martti Ahtisaari Peace Foundation has won a prize for innovation in mediation and conflict management for its AI-supported consultation that increased young people’s participation in its work with Yemeni political parties.

Felix Kufus (fourth left) at the prize ceremony. He led CMI’s development and implementation of the approach.

The prize by the Round Table for Mediation and Conflict Management of the German Economy recognises innovative approaches that promote alternative dispute resolution or conflict prevention.

Eligible innovations could be procedural, substantive, technical or non-technical, but had to be theoretically grounded, already applied in practice and respond to a recognisable demand.

“Digital innovation is most valuable when it helps us hear voices that might otherwise go unheard,” said Johanna Poutanen, Head of CMI’s Inclusion and Digital Innovation team.

title: Youth perspectives on polarisation: When does difference become division? Join us for a webinar on 21 September
content:
As part of the annual Youth Peace Week Finland’s programme and to mark the International Day of Peace, CMI brings together a panel of voices from Armenia, Finland and Palestine to discuss youth perspectives on polarisation. The webinar is open to all through registration and will take place on Monday, 21 September 2026, at 15:00–16:15 EEST.

The webinar examines polarisation from a youth perspective across three distinct contexts: Armenia, Finland, and Palestine. The panel aims to unpack the key drivers of polarisation in each context, young people’s experiences of living in polarised environments, and the implications of polarisation for social cohesion and peace in society. It also explores how young people may actively contest, counter, or contribute to polarisation.

15:00–15:10 Opening remarks by Johanna Poutanen, Head of Inclusion and Digital Innovation, CMI – Martti Ahtisaari Peace Foundation

15:10–16:00 Panel discussion:

title: Creating space for youth dialogue in Palestine
content:
CMI is working with young people across the West Bank and Gaza to support constructive dialogue about the future of Palestine.

A newly launched three-year initiative in the West Bank and Gaza focuses on engaging young Palestinians in structured and inclusive dialogue on the future of Palestine, with the aim of strengthening their political agency in peacemaking.

The initiative, implemented in partnership with the Palestine-based Social Developmental Forum (SDF), responds to youth’s fragmentation, shrinking civic space and generational exclusion from decision-making.

It is co-funded by the European Union, the Ministry for Foreign Affairs of Finland and Ireland and runs from 2025 to 2028. Its inception phase in 2025 was supported by Ireland and Sweden through their core funding to CMI, with additional support continuing through core funding.

In the first phase, a series of dialogue workshops aim to reach 700 young people across the West Bank and Gaza. In the following phase, participants will connect, learn, and engage in discussions through secure online and in-person formats, supported by digital consultations.

title: CMI’s CEO Janne Taalas appointed Permanent Representative of Finland to the United Nations
content:
After serving as CEO of CMI – Martti Ahtisaari Peace Foundation for more than five years, Janne Taalas will leave his position following a period of significant transformation and growth for the organisation. The President of the Republic of Finland Alexander Stubb has appointed Taalas as Permanent Representative of Finland to the United Nations in New York as of 1 November 2026. CMI’s Board will launch the process to appoint a new CEO without delay.

“Janne Taalas has led CMI through an exceptionally turbulent period, as war, geopolitical fragmentation, and technological change have transformed the environment for peacemaking. Under his leadership, CMI has successfully adapted its work to a changing world and strengthened its position as a trusted and effective peacemaking partner,” says Marko Ahtisaari, CMI’s Chair of the Board.

title: What is UN Peacebuilding Week? Q&A with CMI’s Natalia Martinez Cutillas
content:
In June this year CMI attended the UN’s first Peacebuilding Week in New York. But why was CMI invited and how does attendance support the organisation’s goals? We spoke to Natalia Martinez Cutillas of CMI’s Multilateral Affairs and Peacemaking Policy team to find out more.

Natalia Martinez Cutillas: When the UN Peacebuilding Architecture was established in 2005, Member States agreed that it should be reviewed every five years to ensure it remained fit for purpose. This process, known as the UN Peacebuilding Architecture Review (PBAR), most recently took place in 2025. As part of the outcome of that review, Member States mandated that an annual UN Peacebuilding Week should be organised.

The idea behind the week was to shine a spotlight on the UN’s peacebuilding work, build political support for peacebuilding efforts, create space for inclusive dialogue and showcase good practices from around the world.

title: Moldova study: women’s meaningful participation is essential for sustainable peace
content:
Women in the Autonomous Territorial Unit (ATU) of Gagauzia already play pivotal roles in sustaining dialogue, strengthening community resilience, and preventing conflict. However, their experience, perspectives and leadership remain insufficiently represented in formal dialogue, peacebuilding and decision-making mechanisms.

A new locally grounded study published by CMI and the Platform for Security and Defence Initiatives identifies the barriers behind this gap and demonstrates that strengthening women’s meaningful participation is essential for building sustainable peace and social cohesion in the region.

Marina Danoyan (centre), CMI, says the organisation strives to connect women leaders, organisations and movements with the spaces where decisions are actually made.

The study, ‘The Role of Women in Peace Processes: Needs and Prospects for ATU Gagauzia’, was presented on 10 July in Chisinau during a roundtable convening representatives of public institutions, international organisations, diplomatic missions, civil society, and experts on peace, security and gender equality.

title: Strengthening multilateral partnerships for peace: CMI at the first UN Peacebuilding Week
content:
Multilateralism is under increasing strain, armed conflicts are multiplying and attention is shifting from peacebuilding to traditional defence. With the political and civic space for inclusive peacebuilding shrinking, opportunities for dialogue between policy-shapers and those building peace on the ground are in decline.

Against this backdrop, strengthening international cooperation for sustainable peace is critical. This pursuit is at the heart of CMI’s mission, with multilateral cooperation long a central part of the organisation’s work. These principles guided President Martti Ahtisaari when he founded CMI and they continue to drive CMI’s engagement in 2026.

In June, CMI participated in the inaugural UN Peacebuilding Week in New York, organised by the UN Peacebuilding and Peace Support Office (PBPSO) under the theme UN Peacebuilding @20 – Partnerships for Innovation, Inclusion and Impact.

The week marked the 20th anniversary of the UN Peacebuilding Architecture and provided an important opportunity to reflect on progress made over the past two decades, including how peacebuilding must adapt to an increasingly fragmented geopolitical environment.

title: How do mediators construct legitimacy? Insights from Sarah Stroup, CMI’s first academic-in-residence
content:
Professor Sarah Stroup joined CMI as its first Academic-in-Residence, bringing together scholarly research and mediation practice. During her residency in 2025–2026, she explored how private mediation actors establish legitimacy and present themselves as credible third parties in conflict settings. In this conversation, she reflects on her research findings, the evolving mediation landscape, and what she learned from working inside a mediation organisation.

I have been studying non-governmental organisations for about 25 years and have always wanted to do research that speaks to both theoretical and policy questions. My interest in the practical side really shifted when I began building my own skills in conflict facilitation, conflict response, and mediation.

At Middlebury, I directed a conflict transformation collaborative, and through that I learned about the challenges of supporting people as a third party when they are dealing with community and personal conflicts. That experience made me very interested in digging more deeply into the world of mediation NGOs.

title: “Maghreb-Sahel connectivity is an avenue for stability” – CMI’s latest Insight on Sahelo-Saharan peacemaking
content:
The authors of CMI’s latest Insight Paper argue that recognising the interconnected nature of the Maghreb and the Sahel is essential to developing more effective approaches to peace and stability across the region.

Many stakeholders and regional and international actors continue to approach the Sahelo-Saharan space through fragmented, disconnected frameworks, say the authors of CMI’s latest Insight Paper, The Maghreb-Sahel security complex: the necessity of a cross-regional approach to peacemaking.

The paper argues that the Maghreb and the Sahel should be understood as a single regional security complex, where political, security and socio-economic dynamics are deeply intertwined. Yet peacemaking efforts have largely treated the two regions separately, overlooking the connectivity that could instead serve as a catalyst for peace.

Since 2023, CMI has adopted a cross-regional approach to the Maghreb and the Sahel aimed at overcoming siloed approaches to peace and security. This has included bringing together senior experts and think tanks from across both regions to explore dialogue and cooperation in the Sahelo-Saharan space.
